 Social Security Faces a 22% Benefit Cut in 2032 – What Millennials and Gen Z Need to Know
 Sweety 
 October 25, 2026 
 USA News Social Security 
 Social Security benefits could face a potential 22% reduction in 2032 if trust fund reserves are depleted and lawmakers do not act. Millions of Americans could receive higher Social Security payments in 2027, but the program’s longer-term financial outlook presents a different challenge. According to the 2026 Social Security trustees report cited in the supplied information, the retirement and survivors trust fund is projected to run out of reserves in late 2032. If lawmakers do not act, incoming revenue would be sufficient to cover only about 78% of scheduled benefits at that point.
 That could translate into an effective 22% reduction in scheduled retirement and survivors benefits. For younger workers, including millennials and Generation Z, the projections raise questions about future retirement income, payroll taxes, and whether Congress will make changes before the funding deadline.
 One possible solution would be to increase the payroll tax that funds Social Security. An analysis by the conservative advocacy group Advancing American Freedom estimates that maintaining scheduled benefits through payroll tax increases alone could require raising the combined rate from 12.4% to 17.3% by 2034. That would represent an increase of roughly 40% in the tax rate, although the actual cost to individual workers would depend on the policy adopted.
 These figures describe projections and possible policy responses, not changes that have already been enacted. Knowing the difference is essential when assessing what Social Security’s financial outlook means for today’s workers and retirees.

 COLA 
 The Social Security Administration (SSA) announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027, according to the supplied report. The increase is designed to help benefits keep pace with inflation and will take effect in January 2027 for most Social Security recipients.
 Based on the agency’s reported estimates, the average monthly retirement benefit would rise from approximately $2,095 to $2,170, an increase of about $75.
 The adjustment also affects people receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI), a separate program that provides payments to eligible older adults and people with qualifying disabilities or limited income and resources. According to the supplied information, higher SSI payments will begin on December 31, 2026, for approximately 7.3 million recipients.
 The SSA estimates that the increase will reach around 76 million Americans across Social Security and SSI, including people who receive both types of payments.
 COLAs are calculated using changes in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W. The measure tracks price changes experienced by a particular group of workers and is used to determine annual adjustments to Social Security benefits.
 However, a COLA does not necessarily mean that retirees will experience an equivalent improvement in their purchasing power. Housing, healthcare, groceries, insurance, and other household expenses may rise at different rates. Some beneficiaries may find that their increased payments are largely absorbed by higher living costs.
 The annual increase and the trust fund outlook also address different issues. A COLA adjusts payments to account for inflation, while the trust fund projections concern whether the program will have sufficient resources to pay all scheduled benefits over time.
 Readers can check official announcements and benefit information through the Social Security Administration .
 Forecast 
 The central concern is the projected depletion of the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund, which finances retirement and survivors benefits.
 According to the 2026 trustees report cited in the supplied material, the OASI fund is projected to exhaust its reserves in the fourth quarter of 2032. After that point, payroll taxes and other incoming revenue would cover approximately 78% of scheduled benefits if Congress had not enacted changes to the program.
 The difference between 100% of scheduled benefits and 78% is the basis for the projected 22% shortfall.
 Social Security measure Projection 
 OASI trust fund depletion Fourth quarter of 2032 
 Scheduled benefits covered after depletion 78% 
 Potential shortfall in scheduled benefits 22% 
 Combined OASDI trust fund depletion Third quarter of 2034 
 Combined fund benefit coverage after depletion 83% 
 The combined Old-Age and Survivors Insurance and Disability Insurance (OASDI) trust funds are projected to reach depletion later, in the third quarter of 2034. At that point, incoming revenue would cover an estimated 83% of scheduled benefits.
 These projections are not identical because the retirement and survivors program and the disability insurance program have separate trust funds, while the combined measure considers them together.
 The distinction matters because a combined trust fund projection can make the program’s financial outlook appear less immediate than the projection for the retirement and survivors fund alone.
 The trustees’ report also projects that the share of scheduled benefits covered by incoming revenue could decline further over subsequent decades if lawmakers do not change the financing structure.
 The official report is available in the 2026 Social Security trustees report .
 Meaning 
 Trust fund depletion does not mean Social Security will stop collecting payroll taxes or paying benefits altogether.
 The program receives ongoing revenue from payroll taxes and other sources. Even after reserves are exhausted, those revenues would continue to finance a substantial portion of scheduled benefits.
 The problem is that the projected revenue would not be sufficient to pay the full amount currently scheduled under the law.
 If Congress does not change the system before reserves are depleted, benefit payments would face a shortfall unless another legal or administrative mechanism provided additional funding. The exact effect on individual recipients would depend on how the shortfall was implemented and whether lawmakers changed the rules.
 For a retired household receiving $2,000 per month in scheduled benefits, a hypothetical 22% reduction would equal $440 per month, leaving $1,560. This example illustrates the potential scale of the reduction; it is not a prediction of the actual payment any particular beneficiary would receive.
 The effects could be particularly difficult for retirees who depend on Social Security for most of their income. People with limited savings may have fewer options to absorb a reduction than households with pensions, investment accounts, or other sources of income.
 Younger workers face a different concern. They may have decades before retirement, but the decisions made now could influence the payroll taxes they pay and the benefits available when they eventually claim Social Security.
 Taxes 
 One possible response would be to increase the payroll tax used to finance Social Security.
 Under the current structure described in the supplied material, the combined payroll tax rate is 12.4% of covered earnings. Employees generally pay 6.2%, while employers contribute another 6.2%. Self-employed workers generally pay both shares, subject to applicable rules and deductions.
 The tax applies only up to an annual maximum amount of covered earnings. According to the supplied report, that taxable maximum is scheduled to increase from $184,500 in 2026 to $192,300 in 2027.
 Advancing American Freedom estimates that maintaining scheduled benefits through higher payroll taxes alone could require raising the combined rate to 17.3% by 2034.
 Payroll tax scenario Combined rate Change from 12.4% 
 Current rate described in the report 12.4% Baseline 
 Earlier increase proposed in the analysis 16.65% About 34% higher 
 Rate estimated for 2034 17.3% About 40% higher 
 These figures represent scenarios from an advocacy group’s analysis, not a tax increase approved by Congress or an official recommendation adopted by the Social Security trustees.
 The distinction is important because the required tax rate depends on assumptions about future wages, employment, demographics, economic growth, and the timing of any policy changes.
 A 40% increase in the tax rate would also not mean that every worker’s entire income tax burden would rise by 40%. It refers to the relative increase in the Social Security payroll tax rate, from 12.4% to 17.3%.
 For an employee whose earnings are fully subject to the payroll tax, a higher combined rate could increase the employee’s share if the increase were divided equally between workers and employers. The employer’s contribution would rise as well, although the broader economic effects could extend beyond the direct tax payment.
 Generations 
 Millennials and Generation Z have a particular reason to pay attention to Social Security’s long-term finances: they have more time before retirement, but their working years will help finance benefits for current retirees.
 Social Security operates largely on a pay-as-you-go basis. Payroll taxes collected from today’s workers help fund benefits paid to current beneficiaries, while trust fund reserves help cover the difference when program costs exceed incoming revenue.
 Demographic changes contribute to the funding challenge. As the population ages, the number of people receiving retirement benefits changes relative to the number of workers paying into the system. Longer life expectancy and changes in birth rates can influence this relationship, along with wage growth and employment.
 Younger workers therefore face two broad uncertainties. Congress could raise taxes or adjust other parts of the program to improve its finances. Alternatively, lawmakers could change benefit formulas, eligibility rules, or other provisions to reduce future costs.
 A combination of changes is also possible.
 It would be premature to conclude that millennials and Gen Z will receive no Social Security benefits. The projections instead indicate that, under current law and the assumptions used in the trustees’ report, scheduled benefits would exceed the resources available after trust fund depletion.
 For younger households, the practical response is to avoid relying exclusively on a single forecast when planning for retirement. Building savings, considering workplace retirement plans, and understanding expected expenses can help reduce financial uncertainty.
 At the same time, private savings are not a direct substitute for Social Security’s role in providing retirement, disability, and survivor protection. The program remains an important component of retirement security for workers across generations.
 Options 
 Congress has several broad options for addressing Social Security’s financial shortfall. Each involves trade-offs, and the trustees’ projections do not require lawmakers to choose one particular solution.
 Higher revenue: Lawmakers could increase payroll tax rates, change the taxable earnings cap, or explore other ways to increase revenue. These measures could strengthen program finances, but the effects would vary depending on how the changes were structured.
 Benefit adjustments: Congress could change the formula used to calculate future benefits, modify certain eligibility rules, or make other adjustments to spending. The impact would depend on which groups were affected and whether existing beneficiaries or future retirees were treated differently.
 A combined approach: Policymakers could distribute the adjustment between revenue increases and benefit changes. Gradual changes introduced well before the projected depletion dates could provide more time for workers, employers, and retirees to plan.
 The trade-offs extend beyond government accounting. Higher payroll taxes could reduce take-home pay for workers and increase employment costs for businesses. Benefit adjustments could create financial pressure for retirees, particularly those with limited alternative income.
 The timing of reforms matters as well. Acting earlier could spread changes over a longer period, while delaying decisions could leave lawmakers with fewer options as the projected depletion dates approach.
 The Social Security Administration’s actuarial projections provide further information about the program’s long-term finances and projected benefit coverage.
 Commissioner 
 Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano has expressed confidence that the program will continue operating for decades.
 In an interview with CNBC on October 12, ahead of the 2027 COLA announcement, Bisignano said Social Security would be around for another 90 years. He also discussed efforts to improve the agency’s operations and correct inaccurate records.
 His comments reflect the administration’s stated commitment to maintaining the program. However, assurances about Social Security’s long-term existence do not eliminate the funding shortfall identified by the trustees.
 The program can continue operating while still facing a gap between scheduled benefits and projected revenue. The central policy question is how that gap will be addressed before the trust funds reach depletion.
 Bisignano declined to discuss potential changes to benefits or the taxes that finance the program, according to the supplied report. As a result, his comments do not establish which policy measures, if any, the administration will support.

 Outlook 
 Social Security’s financial outlook presents a challenge that extends beyond the next annual cost-of-living adjustment. The projected 3.6% increase in 2027 could provide some relief to beneficiaries facing higher prices, but it does not resolve the program’s long-term funding imbalance.
 The 2026 trustees’ projections indicate that the retirement and survivors trust fund could exhaust its reserves in late 2032, leaving incoming revenue sufficient to cover about 78% of scheduled benefits. A separate projection for the combined retirement, survivors, and disability trust funds points to depletion in 2034.
 Those dates are projections, not guarantees that benefits will be reduced by a specific amount. Congress can change the program’s financing and benefit rules before the projected deadlines.
 For millennials and Gen Z, the potential payroll tax increase illustrates one of the financial choices policymakers may face. But the 17.3% rate is an estimate from an advocacy group’s analysis, not an enacted tax rate or a settled policy outcome.
 The central issue is whether lawmakers will adopt a combination of revenue changes and benefit reforms before the funding gap becomes an immediate payment constraint. Until those decisions are made, workers and retirees should distinguish official projections from policy proposals and plan for retirement with a clear understanding of both Social Security and their other sources of income.
